title: DSSSB Memory Management & Related Concepts - Complete Practice Test

questions.q: The stack memory area is primarily used for storing:
options: Function call frames, local variables, and return addresses

questions.q: Heap memory is primarily used for:
options: Dynamically allocated memory during program execution

questions.q: Memory allocation and deallocation on the stack is managed:
Memory allocation on the heap is managed:
options: Manually by the programmer (allocated and freed explicitly)

questions.q: Compared to heap allocation, stack allocation is generally:
options: Faster, due to simple pointer increment/decrement

questions.q: A stack overflow typically occurs due to:
options: Excessive or infinite recursion consuming stack space

questions.q: Which of the following is stored on the stack in a typical function call?
Heap memory, unlike stack memory, is generally:
options: Limited to a fixed small size determined at compile time
Larger and more flexible, but slower to allocate/deallocate

questions.q: Fragmentation is a memory issue most commonly associated with:
The lifetime of a stack-allocated local variable ends when:
options: The function/block in which it is declared returns

questions.q: Which memory area is typically thread-specific (each thread gets its own)?
Accessing a stack variable's address after its function has returned results in:
options: Undefined behavior, since the memory may be reused

questions.q: Which memory region typically has a fixed maximum size set by the OS or compiler at thread creation?
Which of the following operations is generally NOT associated with heap memory?
Function call information such as return address and saved registers is stored in a structure called:
Heap memory access is generally slower than stack access mainly because:
options: Heap memory uses a simple pointer bump for allocation
Heap allocation involves more complex bookkeeping to find suitable free blocks
Heap memory is always on a remote disk
Stack memory does not exist in most systems

questions.q: In a multi-threaded program, the heap is typically:
options: Shared among all threads of the process

questions.q: Excessively large local arrays declared inside a function can cause:
options: Compile-time-only errors with no runtime effect

questions.q: Which of the following is true about the relative growth direction of stack and heap in many system memory layouts?
options: Both grow in the same direction from the same starting address
The stack and heap typically grow toward each other from opposite ends of the address space
Only the heap grows; the stack is fixed

questions.q: Recursive functions with deep recursion primarily consume additional memory from the:
options: Stack, due to repeated stack frame creation

questions.q: Which of the following best describes 'automatic' variables in C in relation to memory?
options: They are allocated on the heap and must be freed manually
They are allocated on the stack and automatically deallocated when their scope ends
They persist for the entire program duration
They are stored in the code segment

questions.q: Static memory allocation means memory is allocated:
options: At runtime based on user input
At compile time, with a fixed size

questions.q: Dynamic memory allocation means memory is allocated:
options: At runtime, as needed by the program

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of static memory allocation?
options: int arr[10]; declared inside a function

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of dynamic memory allocation?
A key advantage of dynamic memory allocation is:
options: Flexibility to allocate memory size based on runtime requirements
It is always faster than static allocation
No need to manage memory at all

questions.q: A key disadvantage of dynamic memory allocation is:
options: The programmer is responsible for freeing memory, risking leaks
It cannot be used with structures
It always wastes more memory than static allocation

questions.q: In static memory allocation, the size of data structures must be known:
Global and static variables in C are typically stored in:
Which allocation type is generally more memory-efficient when the exact size requirement is unknown beforehand?
Which of the following is a limitation of static memory allocation?
options: It adapts automatically to changing data sizes at runtime
The array or data structure size cannot be changed once compiled

questions.q: In C, the keyword used to allocate memory that persists for the program's lifetime and is initialized once is:
Which statement about resizing memory dynamically is correct?
options: Statically allocated arrays can be resized using realloc()
Dynamically allocated memory (via malloc/calloc) can be resized using realloc()
Neither static nor dynamic memory can ever be resized
Resizing is only possible for stack variables

questions.q: A program that reads an unknown number of records from a file at runtime would most appropriately use:
options: Dynamic memory allocation to grow storage as needed

questions.q: Which of the following best contrasts static and dynamic allocation in terms of control?
options: Static gives the programmer runtime control; dynamic gives compile-time control
Static size is fixed at compile time; dynamic size and lifetime are controlled by the programmer at runtime
Both are identical in terms of control

questions.q: Which of these is typically allocated statically in a C program?
options: A node created via malloc() in a linked list
A global array declared with a fixed size

questions.q: One reason dynamic allocation can be riskier than static allocation is:
options: It requires explicit management, increasing risk of leaks or dangling pointers
It is not supported in C
It always uses more memory than needed

questions.q: Which of the following is an advantage of static allocation over dynamic allocation?
options: It is simpler and avoids the overhead and risks of manual memory management
It always uses less total memory
It supports variable-length arrays without any restriction

questions.q: A variable declared with the static keyword inside a function, in terms of memory, behaves most like:
options: A stack variable that disappears after the function returns
A variable with a fixed memory location for the program's duration, similar to global storage

questions.q: Which allocation approach is more appropriate for implementing a dynamically growing linked list?
A key trade-off when choosing dynamic allocation over static allocation is:
options: Greater flexibility in size/lifetime at the cost of manual memory management overhead
No trade-off exists between the two
Dynamic allocation always uses less code

questions.q: Which of these best describes memory allocated with the 'new' operator in C++?
options: Dynamically allocated on the heap and must be released with 'delete'

questions.q: A memory leak occurs when:
options: Memory is allocated and properly freed
Dynamically allocated memory is no longer needed but never freed
A pointer is set to NULL after use

questions.q: A common cause of memory leaks in C is:
options: Forgetting to call free() on dynamically allocated memory

questions.q: A dangling pointer is created when:
options: A pointer is initialized to NULL
The memory a pointer refers to is freed or goes out of scope, but the pointer still references it
A pointer is assigned a valid new address
Two pointers point to the same valid object

questions.q: Which practice helps prevent dangling pointers after freeing memory?
options: Setting the pointer to NULL immediately after freeing it

questions.q: Dereferencing a dangling pointer typically results in:
options: Undefined behavior, such as a crash or corrupted data

questions.q: Which of the following tools/techniques is commonly used to detect memory leaks in C/C++?
options: Valgrind or similar memory profiling tools

questions.q: A double-free error occurs when:
options: Memory is allocated twice for the same pointer
free() is called twice on the same memory block

questions.q: Long-running programs (like servers) are particularly vulnerable to:
options: Gradual memory leaks that degrade performance over time

questions.q: Which of the following best prevents memory leaks in dynamically allocated linked structures?
options: Ensuring every allocated node is freed when no longer needed

questions.q: A wild pointer differs from a dangling pointer in that a wild pointer:
options: Is uninitialized and points to an unknown/random memory location

questions.q: Which scenario is most likely to cause a memory leak?
options: Calling free() immediately after malloc() when memory is no longer needed
Losing the only pointer reference to allocated memory before freeing it
Setting a pointer to NULL after freeing it

questions.q: In garbage-collected languages (like Java), memory leaks can still occur when:
options: All objects are automatically freed instantly
Objects are still referenced (e.g., in a collection) even though they are no longer needed
The garbage collector is disabled permanently

questions.q: Which of the following is the safest practice when working with dynamically allocated memory?
options: Never checking if malloc() returned NULL
Always pairing each allocation with a corresponding deallocation and avoiding reuse after freeing
Freeing memory multiple times to be safe

questions.q: A common symptom of a memory leak in a long-running application is:
options: Gradually increasing memory consumption over time

questions.q: Using a pointer to access an array element after the array's dynamically allocated memory has been freed is an example of:
options: Dangling pointer usage, leading to undefined behavior

questions.q: If a function returns a pointer to a local (automatic) variable, the safest fix is to:
options: Return the pointer as-is; it is always valid
Allocate the variable dynamically (e.g., with malloc) or pass a buffer from the caller

questions.q: Which of the following can help detect dangling pointer usage during development?
options: Using memory debugging tools and setting freed pointers to NULL
Avoiding the use of any pointers

questions.q: In smart pointer usage (e.g., C++ unique_ptr/shared_ptr), the primary benefit for memory management is:
options: Manual tracking of every allocation is still required
Automatic memory deallocation when the pointer goes out of scope, reducing leaks and dangling pointers
They eliminate the need for a heap entirely
They only work with static memory

questions.q: Returning the address of a local variable from a function is a common cause of:
options: Dangling pointers, since the local variable's stack memory is invalid after return

questions.q: A shallow copy of an object copies:
options: Only primitive fields, creating new copies of all referenced objects too
The top-level fields, but referenced objects/pointers are shared between original and copy
Nothing; it is identical to a deep copy

questions.q: A deep copy of an object copies:
options: Only the reference/pointer to nested objects
The object and recursively all objects it references, creating fully independent copies

questions.q: A key risk of shallow copying is:
options: Both copies sharing the same underlying dynamic memory, so changes in one affect the other

questions.q: When two shallow-copied objects both go out of scope, their destructors freeing the same shared pointer will most likely cause:
Deep copy is generally preferred over shallow copy when:
options: The object contains no pointers or dynamically allocated members
The object contains pointers/dynamic memory that must be independently owned by each copy

questions.q: In C++, the default copy constructor performs:
To implement deep copy behavior in a C++ class with pointer members, a programmer typically needs to:
options: Rely entirely on the default copy constructor
Explicitly define a custom copy constructor (and often assignment operator) that allocates new memory

questions.q: If two objects share the same dynamically allocated memory due to a shallow copy, freeing memory in one object's destructor can lead to:
options: A dangling pointer or double-free issue in the other object
No effect on the other object

questions.q: Which of the following is true regarding shallow copy performance compared to deep copy?
options: Shallow copy is generally faster since it does not duplicate nested data

questions.q: In Python, which module/function is commonly used to perform a deep copy of an object?
When an object containing only primitive (non-pointer) data members is copied, shallow copy and deep copy produce:
options: Effectively the same result, since there are no shared references to worry about

questions.q: In Java, the default behavior of Object.clone() performs:
options: A deep copy of all fields automatically
A shallow copy by default unless overridden

questions.q: If a class has a raw pointer member pointing to dynamically allocated memory, relying on the compiler-generated copy constructor risks:
options: Automatic deep copying with no issues
Multiple objects sharing and potentially double-freeing the same memory
Loss of the pointer's data type

questions.q: The 'Rule of Three' in C++ suggests that if a class defines one of the destructor, copy constructor, or copy assignment operator, it should generally define:
options: All three, to properly manage resources like deep copies

questions.q: A deep copy is generally more expensive than a shallow copy in terms of:
options: Time and memory, since it duplicates all nested data

questions.q: Which technique can be used in C++ to allocate independent memory for each object during a deep copy?
options: Allocating new memory and copying the pointed-to data's contents

questions.q: When would a shallow copy be an acceptable and efficient choice?
options: When the object owns dynamically allocated resources that must not be shared
When the object contains only simple, non-owning data with no dynamic resources
Never, deep copy should always be used

questions.q: Object copying issues due to shallow copies are most critical for classes that manage:
options: Dynamically allocated resources such as memory, file handles, or network connections

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes a deep copy's independence from the original object?
options: Changes to the copy affect the original object
Changes to the copy do not affect the original object, since all nested data is duplicated
Deep copies and originals always occupy the same memory

questions.q: The copy assignment operator, if not explicitly defined for a class with dynamic memory members, will by default perform:
options: A shallow (member-wise) copy, similar to the default copy constructor

questions.q: Object slicing in C++ occurs when:
options: A derived class object is assigned to a base class object, losing derived-class-specific members
A base class object is converted to a derived class object

questions.q: Object slicing typically happens when objects are passed or assigned:
options: By value, from a derived class to a base class type

questions.q: Which of the following helps avoid object slicing when working with polymorphic classes?
options: Using pointers or references to the base class instead of passing by value

questions.q: After object slicing occurs, which part of the derived object is lost?
options: The additional members and overridden behavior specific to the derived class

questions.q: Object slicing is most relevant in the context of:
options: Polymorphism and inheritance in object-oriented languages like C++

questions.q: If a function parameter is declared to take a base class object by value, passing a derived class object will result in:
options: Full preservation of derived class data
Object slicing, retaining only the base class part

questions.q: Storing derived class objects by value in a container of base class type (e.g., a vector of base objects) will result in:
options: Object slicing for each stored element
A compile-time error in all cases

questions.q: Which container/approach is recommended to store polymorphic objects of different derived types safely?
options: A container of base class objects by value
A container of pointers (or smart pointers) to the base class
A union of all derived types
A static array of base class objects only

questions.q: After object slicing, calling a virtual function on the sliced object will invoke:
options: The base class's version, since the derived part was sliced away
No function at all, causing a crash

questions.q: Object slicing is generally considered:
options: A desirable feature to simplify code
An unintended and often problematic side effect that programmers should avoid

questions.q: Assigning a derived class object to an already existing base class object (not through a pointer/reference) will:
options: Only copy the base class members, slicing off the rest
Cause a runtime exception in all languages
Automatically convert the base object into a derived object

questions.q: Which C++ feature, when combined with pass-by-value, makes object slicing a notable concern?
A common fix for object slicing when a function needs to operate polymorphically on an object is to change the parameter from pass-by-value to:
Which of the following statements about object slicing is true?
options: It only affects primitive data types
It occurs specifically with object composition, not assignment or parameter passing
It results in loss of derived-class data when a derived object is treated as a base object by value
It improves performance with no downsides

questions.q: Returning a derived class object by value from a function whose return type is declared as the base class will result in:
options: The full derived object being returned intact
Object slicing, returning only the base class portion

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical consequence of object slicing?
options: Loss of derived class member data
Loss of derived class overridden behavior when accessed through the sliced object
Automatic memory leak in every case
The object effectively behaving as a base class instance

questions.q: A defensive coding practice to detect potential slicing issues during design is to:
options: Mark classes not meant to be sliced as non-copyable or use pointers/references for polymorphic use
Always pass objects by value for simplicity

questions.q: Object slicing can be safely avoided when a derived object is explicitly assigned to a base class pointer (not object) because:
options: The pointer only stores an address, so the full derived object remains intact in memory
Pointers automatically convert derived objects into base objects
Pointers cannot reference derived class objects
Slicing always occurs regardless of pointer or value usage

questions.q: Which scenario best illustrates object slicing with function arguments?
options: A function taking a base class pointer as a parameter
A function taking a base class object by value, called with a derived class argument
A function taking a base class reference as a parameter
A function using a template parameter
